the development of a model that will account for the behavior of organisms in a wide range of situations, including those in which the organism must make complex decisions and those that require it to learn complex stimulus relations.

the behavior of the animal is controlled to differing degrees by both the discriminative stimulus—behavior relation and the reinforcer—behavior relation.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the concurrent three-term operant contingency is the fundamental unit of behavior.

the model is a quantitative description of behavior in a wide variety of experimental procedures, that the parameters of the model can be interpreted as indices of behavior, that the model is consistent with the notion that behavior is controlled by the environment, and that the model is not consistent with the notion of a separate mechanism for the control of behavior.
the behavior of an animal in a given situation is a function of its history of reinforcement and of its current sensory input.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the stimulus—behavior and the behavior—reinforcement relations are both important in the analysis of operant behavior, and that the two relations interact.
behavior is controlled by both stimulus—response and response—outcome relationships.
behavior is not controlled by the presence of reinforcers or stimuli, but rather by the relations that exist between stimuli and reinforcers.
